title: Shannon’s Demon, Made Exact (Part 1)
text:
Introduction
If intuition is any guide, it shouldn’t be possible for a long-only portfolio to be profitable when each of its component assets is a major loser, unless, of course, one is clairvoyant and can predict those fleeting moments when random chance will favor each asset. Yet, as I’ll demonstrate in this post, not only is this possible but also an investor can (almost surely) guarantee an exponential amount of money in the long run from such a portfolio, if he knows what he’s doing. It turns out that information theory provides a lovely explanation for why this is the case.


The setup
Consider a two-asset portfolio consisting of a riskless asset and a risky asset. We will think of the riskless asset as analogous to a Swiss bank account: the account is so safe and so desirable that it pays a negative interest rate; hence, its associated gross return satisfies \(r < 1.\) On the other hand, the risky asset, which I’ll model as a fair coin flip, will be highly volatile in its outcome, where heads comes with a very handsome return and tails with a very steep loss. When the coin flip comes up heads, the risky asset will have a gross return of \(\gamma_h\) for heads and \(\gamma_t < r < \gamma_h\) for tails. In addition, I’ll let \(p_h\) denote the probability of heads, and I’ll set \(\gamma_t = \alpha/\gamma_h\), for some \(\alpha > 0\). Finally, I let \(f\) denote the fraction of our money that we allocate to the risky asset, and \(1 - f\) the fraction that we allocate to the riskless asset. Our goal is to choose \(f\) intelligently. (The reader should pause for a moment to convince himself that \(r\) must be between \(\gamma_t\) and \(\gamma_h\) for this game to be interesting.)
For the specific example below, I’ll set:

\(r = 0.97\): a negative interest rate of 3% per period.
\(\gamma_h = 2\): a 100% net gain on heads.
\(p_h = 0.5\): it’s a fair coin.
\(\alpha = 0.8\): this implies \(\gamma_t = 0.4\), i.e. a 60% net loss on tails.



Show code
from coin_flip_with_riskless_asset_model import CoinFlipWithRisklessAssetModel
coin_flip_model = CoinFlipWithRisklessAssetModel(r=0.97, gamma_heads=2.0, p=0.5, alpha=0.80)




The risky asset is a major loser
Obviously the riskless asset is a long-term loser, as it bleeds 3% each period. While it is less obvious, the risky asset is also a long-term loser, which is easily seen from Monte Carlo simulations:


Show code
import numpy as np
from finlib.ensemble_of_returns_paths import EnsembleOfReturnsPaths
from finlib.simulating_performance import crp_performance

seed = 12345
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
num_paths = 500
num_periods = 250

weights_for_risky_asset = np.array([0.0, 1.0]) # 0% in riskless, 100% in risky
gross_returns_tensor = coin_flip_model.generate_random_gross_returns(rng, num_periods=num_periods, num_paths=num_paths)
perf_risky_matrix = crp_performance(weights_for_risky_asset, gross_returns_tensor)
ensemble_risky = EnsembleOfReturnsPaths.from_gross(perf_risky_matrix)

growth_rate_summary_df_risky = ensemble_risky.summarize_across_paths(ensemble_risky.running_growth_rate, threshold=0.0) 
wealth_summary_df_risky = ensemble_risky.summarize_across_paths(ensemble_risky.running_wealth_ratio, threshold=1.0) 


The figure below summarizes 500 simulated wealth paths over 250 periods. The periwinkle line is the median outcome and the shaded band the 95% interval; the lime dashed line is the mean, dragged well above the typical path by a lucky few.


                            
                                            




Some initial remarks

With these parameters, the expected gross return of the risky asset in a given period is given by \[\mathbb{E}[\gamma] = p_h \gamma_h + (1 - p_h) \gamma_t = 1.2.\] Not bad at all!
In addition, notice that the gross return of our portfolio in a given period is given by \[Y(f) = (1 - f)r + f\gamma,\] where \(\gamma\) is the random gross return of the risky asset; thus, in expectation, our portfolio’s gross return is given by \[\mathbb{E}[Y(f)] = (1 - f)r + f\mathbb{E}[\gamma] = 0.97 + 0.23f,\] which is greater than 1 for any \(f > 0.13\). So, we can get an expected gross return greater than 1 by putting some (specifically \(f > 0.13\)) of our money in the risky asset.
Because I chose \(\alpha < 1\), however, the geometric mean of the risky asset’s gross returns is much more sobering: \[\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log \gamma]) = 0.8944 < 1.\]

Here is a citation! (Kelly 1956)


References


Kelly, J. L. 1956. “A New Interpretation of Information Rate.” Bell System Technical Journal 35 (4): 917–26.
